Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister says Labor has ‘broadly got the legislation right’ but is open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reform. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Gambling Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ to gambling laws after inquiry hears alcohol and cocaine offered to punters Sources say Albanese government willing to tighten rules on betting inducements but less likely to budge on TV and online advertisements Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Sat 8 Aug 2026 23.58 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 00.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Albanese government is prepared to tighten rules on gambling inducements, but is less likely to budge on advertising rules, as negotiations continue on wagering legislation, which so far has lacked the support needed to pass parliament. Federal Labor is open to considering amendments to its legislation from the Coalition when MPs return to Canberra this week, sources say. The government was prepared to make changes around wagering inducements – a focus of explosive parliamentary hearings last week – as part of negotiations, but was less open to tweaking proposed rules on the frequency of advertisements on TV and online. Additional restrictions on ads are a major demand of gambling harm advocates and the Senate crossbench. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Upper house hearings have aired sensational allegations that wagering companies provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting. Betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp say there is no evidence to substantiate these claims. “If the government’s now willing to move on some things, well, good, but the devil is going to be in the detail,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, a vocal proponent of stronger action, told the ABC on Sunday. “Inducements, of course … should be gone.” The Coalition, crossbenchers and the Greens have opposed Labor’s reforms as proposed by the communications minister, Anika Wells, meaning the legislation is unlikely to pass in its current form. Sources said the government was more inclined to deal with the Coalition and would await amendments from the opposition after its party room met in the nation’s capital this week. The government frontbencher Jenny McAllister said on Sunday that Wells was in discussion with the Coalition and had been “paying attention” to evidence from the recent parliamentary hearings. McAllister said Labor thought it had “broadly got the legislation right” but was open to “sensible amendments”. “We want to see this through the parliament,” she said. Inducements can include perks like “bonus bets”, promotional odds, rebates or more VIP enticements like hospitality at events. Luke Bateman tells inquiry gambling companies gave him drugs and alcohol – video The landmark gambling reform report from late Labor MP Peta Murphy called for a total and immediate ban on inducements and their advertising. That issue has been a key focus for advocates within the Coalition, crossbench and Greens – and even among some Labor MPs who want the government to go further. Gambling companies have opposed changes to inducements. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Hanson-Young, speaking on the Insiders program, suggested she would support the proposed “opt-out” model for online advertising being switched to “opt-in”. Critics have argued streaming platforms would be able to show more ads during breaks in play under Labor’s current plan if they implemented a “triple lock” function including an opt-out feature. Campaigners have also criticised the legislation for allowing three TV ads per hour from 6am to 8.30pm, with a ban during live sport. Wells has previously said the government believes the current proposal strikes the correct “balance” between addressing problem gambling while not unduly penalising media companies and sporting codes which rely on wagering revenue. Labor MP Jerome Laxale last week said he would welcome Labor’s draft laws “being strengthened in the Senate”. The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, said the shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, was negotiating for new controls over inducements. Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, told News24 on Sunday that the Coalition wanted more action to protect children. “Under the government’s proposed bill, it doesn’t limit the capacity to advertise to children, and that’s something that I’m concerned about, making sure that we’ve got the measures that are consistent, appropriate, and also reflecting the changing nature of technology,” he said. Last week’s inquiry heard evidence that gambling ads were being played on Spotify between Disney songs for children . Hanson-Young on Sunday demanded tougher regulation from the government and stated: “If you are not prepared to do what’s needed here, well, we’ll take this out of your hands and we’ll do it in the Senate ourselves.” Explore more on these topics Gambling Australian politics Labor party Coalition news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-protests-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mnvz Relatives of the deceased miners gathered in Minna after learning of the deaths Image: Ibrahim Ndamitso/REUTERS Advertisement Protests erupted in central Nigeria on Friday after 37 people believed to be illegal miners died while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC). Police fired tear gas as dozens of demonstrators, including miners and their relatives, gathered in the central city of Minna, Niger State, armed with sticks and machetes, witnesses reported. Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago told reporters on Thursday that the men had died in custody after being arrested earlier in the week on suspicion of illegal mining. He called the incident "sad" and "tragic," adding that a committee of inquiry into the deaths had been established and was already working. The governor declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for the January elections . The Nigerian government announced on Friday that the commandant of Niger state's civil defense corps had been suspended. "It is an unfortunate incident, however, a full investigation will be conducted while the commandant under whose watch this happened remains suspended," the Minister of Interior said in a statement. What do we know about the incident? The suspected miners were detained in a series of arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday, said Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, head of the NSCDC in Niger, in a statement on Thursday. Aniviye said that although the agency suspects the detainees died of disease, their bodies were sent to a local hospital for a medical examination to determine the cause of death. He did not specify the type of disease. However, according to an intelligence report, "preliminary information suggests the fatalities may have resulted from overcrowding and inadequate ventilation within a detention facility." A 40-second video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men, most of whom appeared to be teenagers. Volunteers wearing gloves stood over the bodies, while veiled women tried to identify their relatives. Dirty gold: Nigeria's toxic water threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Survivors describe a lack of ventilation Dauda Shehu, one of the survivors, told the Associated Press that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell. "We were jampacked and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well," he said. "All of a sudden, we realized that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air," Shehu added. The detainees tried to get the guards' attention by banging on the cell door, he explained. Spanning more than twice the area of Belgium, Niger State is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most of whom are lured by the hope of striking gold. According to officials and experts, the scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger State is also fueling violence by criminal gangs known locally as bandits. These gangs tax miners and demand a cut of the extracted ore in exchange for access to the pits. Edited by: Sean Sinico and Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. Czechia held it from January to June 2009 and from July to December 2022. The presidency chairs meetings and brokers compromises in the Council; it sets no policy alone and does not lead the EU the way a president leads a state. On this page 9 sections What the presidency is Trios and programmes What the presidency does in practice The last presidency under the old rules 2009 and 2022 Why it matters to a resident Why smaller states value the job When is the next one? Following the Council In the autumn of 2022 Prague hosted something it had never held before: a summit of leaders from across the whole continent, not just the EU. The first meeting of the European Political Community took place there on 6 October 2022, during Czechia's second turn at the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU. For a few months Czech civil servants chaired a very long list of meetings in Brussels, and the traffic ran the other way too, with ministers from across Europe coming to Czech cities. The presidency in numbers length of each rotating presidency 6 months span of a trio programme shared by three presidencies 18 months Czech presidencies so far: January to June 2009 and July to December 2022 2 Source: Council of the EU; Government of the Czech Republic (as of 2026; check the official source) What the presidency is The Council of the EU, where ministers of the member states adopt laws with the European Parliament, is chaired by one member state at a time. The chair rotates every six months in an order agreed in advance, so each country gets the job roughly once every 13 and a half years (27 members at six months each). Czechia has had two turns: January to June 2009 and July to December 2022. Two other posts are easily confused with it. The European Council , the summit of leaders, has a permanent president, not a rotating one. And the President of the European Commission leads a separate institution. The rotating presidency is about running the Council's work. How these bodies fit together is in how the EU works . Three posts people mix up Feature Rotating presidency President of the European Council President of the Commission Who A member state's government A person chosen by the leaders A person nominated by the leaders and approved by Parliament Term Six months Fixed term, not rotating Five-year term Chairs Meetings of the Council and its working groups Summits of leaders The Commission As of 2026; check the EU institutions' websites. Trios and programmes Presidencies do not work alone. Three consecutive presidencies form a "trio" and agree a joint 18-month programme, so long files do not stall when one country hands over to the next. Each country then prepares its own six-month programme within that frame and publishes its priorities. What the presidency does in practice The presidency chairs meetings of ministers and the working groups beneath them, an enormous number of sessions. At the Council's formal meetings the minister of the presidency country normally chairs. Foreign affairs meetings are the exception, chaired by the EU's High Representative for foreign policy. The main tasks are to set the agenda and the order of files for the six months, to act as an honest broker among 27 governments, to represent the Council in talks with the Parliament and the Commission (especially the trilogue negotiations on new laws) and to host informal meetings at home. A presidency can speed a file up or slow it down, but it cannot make other governments vote a particular way. Qualified majority voting and the Commission's right of initiative limit what one country can do. It is also expected to stay neutral: a minister in the chair is supposed to look for a deal that works for everyone, not push a national line. The last presidency under the old rules The timing of the first Czech presidency matters. It fell in the first half of 2009, before the Lisbon Treaty took effect on 1 December of that year. Until then the rotating presidency also chaired the summits of leaders and represented the Union abroad. Lisbon created the permanent president of the European Council and gave the High Representative the chair of foreign affairs meetings. The presidency of 2022 therefore worked within a different division of labour from that of 2009. The 2022 presidency also belonged to a trio. It came between France in the first half of 2022 and Sweden in the first half of 2023, and the three countries shared a programme. Czech officials inherited files from Paris and handed their own to Stockholm, and the continuity between them is the point of the system. Two Czech turns in the chair Jan 2009 First presidency begins; it runs to June Mar 2009 The government loses a no-confidence vote; a caretaker cabinet takes over Dec 2009 The Lisbon Treaty takes effect, creating the permanent European Council president Feb 2022 Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine begins Jul 2022 Second presidency begins; it runs to December 6 Oct 2022 First European Political Community summit, in Prague 2009 and 2022 The first Czech presidency, in the first half of 2009, came with an unusual event at home. The Czech government lost a no-confidence vote in March 2009, in the middle of the presidency, and a caretaker government took over for the remainder. The presidency carried on through the change, which is one reason the civil service, rather than the cabinet, does so much of the work. Caretaker cabinets are explained in how a Czech government is formed . The second presidency, in the second half of 2022, ran against the background of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which had begun in February. Energy supply, sanctions, support for Ukraine and for people displaced by the war dominated the agenda, along with the cost of energy. The European Political Community summit in Prague brought together European leaders from beyond the EU as well. The detailed record of what each presidency achieved is published by the government and the EU institutions, and it is the best source for any specific claim. How a presidency runs Trio programme Three consecutive presidencies agree an 18-month plan. National programme The presidency country publishes its own priorities for six months. Chairing the work Ministers chair formal meetings; officials chair the many working groups beneath them. Brokering deals The presidency seeks compromises with Parliament and the Commission, notably in trilogues. Handover Unfinished files pass to the next country in the order. Reading about a presidency, it helps to separate showpieces from substance. Summits and photographs are visible, but the work happens in the working groups, where officials draft compromise texts that ministers later approve. A presidency's real record is the list of files that were closed during its six months, and the presidency's own website and the Council's pages are the places to look for it. Why it matters to a resident A presidency does not change the rules of daily life. It gives a smaller country an unusual window on Brussels and brings meetings, journalists, ministers and officials to its cities, and it forces the national administration to sharpen its handling of EU files. For a foreigner in Prague, the 2022 presidency was visible in road closures around venues, extra security and a level of national coverage of European affairs that rarely appears in other months. Why smaller states value the job A presidency gives a country of Czechia's size an unusual chance to shape agendas. The country in the chair decides the order in which files are taken, chooses the venues of informal ministerial meetings and speaks for the Council in talks with the Parliament. It does this without extra votes, and it is expected to act as a neutral broker, not push a national line. A government that pushes too hard loses the trust of the others, and a presidency lasts only six months. The reward is of a different kind. National civil servants learn how Brussels bargains, a generation of officials gains contacts that last well beyond the term, and ministers become familiar to their counterparts. When the presidency ends, the knowledge stays in the ministries, which is why presidency years are often described as a training ground for the national administration. When is the next one? At 27 members and six months each, the cycle runs about 13 and a half years, so Czechia's next turn falls well into the 2030s. The order of future presidencies is set by a Council decision and published in advance. The Council's published calendar has the exact dates. Following the Council To follow the Council's work, use the website of the current presidency and the Council's own pages, which publish the programme, meeting calendar and outcomes. The Czech government's English pages carry the record of the 2022 presidency. Frequently asked questions How many times has Czechia held the presidency? Twice: January to June 2009 and July to December 2022. Does the presidency country get extra votes? No. Votes in the Council do not change, and the presidency chairs without extra voting weight. Where can I find the current presidency's programme? On the presidency's own website and in the Council's calendar of meetings.
